lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:110" n="3">tu, quod promisti mihi, quod mentita, inimica es;</l>

lines.text: quod nec das et fers saepe, facts facinus.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:110" n="4">quod nec das et fers saepe, facts facinus.</l>

lines.text: aut facere ingenuae est, aut non promisse pudicae,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:110" n="5">aut facere ingenuae est, aut non promisse pudicae,</l>

lines.text: Aufilena, fuit: sed data corripere
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:110" n="6">Aufilena, fuit: sed data corripere</l>

lines.text: fraudando † efficit plus quam meretricis avarae,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:110" n="7">fraudando † efficit plus quam meretricis avarae,</l>

lines.text: quae sese toto corpore prostituit.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:110" n="8">quae sese toto corpore prostituit.</l>

lines.text: Aufilena, viro contentam vivere solo
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:111" n="1">Aufilena, viro contentam vivere solo</l>

lines.text: nuptarum laus e laudibus eximiis:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:111" n="2">nuptarum laus e laudibus eximiis:</l>

lines.text: sed cuivis quamvis potius succumbere par est
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:111" n="3">sed cuivis quamvis potius succumbere par est</l>

lines.text: quam matrem fratres ex patruo parere.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:111" n="4">quam matrem fratres ex patruo parere.</l>

lines.text: Multus homo est, Naso, neque tecum multus homo est qui
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:112" n="1">Multus homo est, Naso, neque tecum multus homo est qui</l>

lines.text: descendit: Naso, multus es et pathicus.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:112" n="2">descendit: Naso, multus es et pathicus.</l>

lines.text: Consule Pompeio primum duo, Cinna, solebant
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:113" n="1">Consule Pompeio primum duo, Cinna, solebant</l>

lines.text: Maeciliam: facto consule nunc iterum
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:113" n="2">Maeciliam: facto consule nunc iterum</l>

lines.text: manserunt duo, sed creverunt milia in unum
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:113" n="3">manserunt duo, sed creverunt milia in unum</l>

lines.text: singula. fecundum semen adulterio.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:113" n="4">singula. fecundum semen adulterio.</l>

lines.text: Firmanus saltu non falso Mentula dives
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:114" n="1">Firmanus saltu non falso Mentula dives</l>

lines.text: fertur, qui tot res in se habet egregias,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:114" n="2">fertur, qui tot res in se habet egregias,</l>

lines.text: aucupium omne genus, piscis, prata, arva, ferasque.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:114" n="3">aucupium omne genus, piscis, prata, arva, ferasque.</l>

lines.text: nequiquam: fructus sumptibus exsuperat.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:114" n="4">nequiquam: fructus sumptibus exsuperat.</l>

lines.text: quare concedo sit dives, dum omnia desint;
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:114" n="5">quare concedo sit dives, dum omnia desint;</l>

lines.text: saltum laudemus, dum domo ipse egeat.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:114" n="6">saltum laudemus, dum domo ipse egeat.</l>

lines.text: Mentula habet iuxta triginta iugera prati,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:115" n="1">Mentula habet iuxta triginta iugera prati,</l>

lines.text: quadraginta arvi: cetera sunt maria.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:115" n="2">quadraginta arvi: cetera sunt maria.</l>

lines.text: cur non divitiis Croesum superare potis sit
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:115" n="3">cur non divitiis Croesum superare potis sit</l>

lines.text: uno qui in saltu tot bona possideat,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:115" n="4">uno qui in saltu tot bona possideat,</l>

lines.text: prata, arva, ingentis silvas saltusque paludesque
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:115" n="5">prata, arva, ingentis silvas saltusque paludesque</l>

lines.text: usque ad Hyperboreos et mare ad Oceanum?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:115" n="6">usque ad Hyperboreos et mare ad Oceanum?</l>

lines.text: omnia magna haec sunt, tamen ipse est maximus ultro,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:115" n="7">omnia magna haec sunt, tamen ipse est maximus ultro,</l>

lines.text: non homo, sed vero mentula magna minax.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:115" n="8">non homo, sed vero mentula magna minax.</l>

lines.text: Saepe tibi studioso animo venante requirens
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:116" n="1">Saepe tibi studioso animo venante requirens</l>

lines.text: carmina uti possem mittere Battiadae
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:116" n="2">carmina uti possem mittere Battiadae</l>

lines.text: qui te lenirem nobis, neu conarere
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:116" n="3">qui te lenirem nobis, neu conarere</l>

lines.text: tela infesta mihi mittere in usque caput,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:116" n="4">tela infesta mihi mittere in usque caput,</l>

lines.text: hunc video mihi nunc frustra sumptum esse laborem,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:116" n="5">hunc video mihi nunc frustra sumptum esse laborem,</l>

lines.text: Gelli, nec nostras hic valuisse preces.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:116" n="6">Gelli, nec nostras hic valuisse preces.</l>

lines.text: contra nos tela ista tua evitamus amictu:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:116" n="7">contra nos tela ista tua evitamus amictu:</l>

lines.text: at fixus nostris tu dabis supplicium.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2:116" n="8">at fixus nostris tu dabis supplicium.</l>

lines.text: To whom inscribe my charming new book—just out and with ashen pumice polished? Cornelius, to you! for you used to deem my triflings of account,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:1" n="1">To whom inscribe my charming new book—just out and with ashen pumice polished? <persName><surname>Cornelius</surname></persName>, to you! for you used to deem my triflings of account, </l>

lines.text: and at a time when you alone of Italians dared unfold the ages’ abstract in three chronicles—learned, by Jupiter!—and most laboriously written. Therefore take this booklet, such as it is, and, O Virgin Patroness,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:1" n="5">and at a time when you alone of Italians dared unfold the ages’ abstract in three chronicles—learned, by <persName><surname>Jupiter</surname></persName>!—and most laboriously written. Therefore take this booklet, such as it is, and, O Virgin Patroness,</l>

lines.text: may it outlive generations more than one.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:1" n="10">may it outlive generations more than one.</l>

lines.text: Sparrow, darling of my girl, with which she plays, which she presses to her bosom, to whom she gives her fingertip, arousing sharp bites as he seeks after it,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:2" n="1">Sparrow, darling of my girl, with which she plays, which she presses to her bosom, to whom she gives her fingertip, arousing sharp bites as he seeks after it,</l>

lines.text: when gleaming with desire of me she jests a light joke of it, so that, I think, it is a solace for her pain when the heavy burning is at rest. Could I but play with you just as she does
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:2" n="5">when gleaming with desire of me she jests a light joke of it, so that, I think, it is a solace for her pain when the heavy burning is at rest. Could I but play with you just as she does</l>

lines.text: and lighten the sad cares of mind. * * * This was as pleasing to me as the golden apple was to the fleet footed girl, which unloosed her girdle long-time fastened.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:2" n="10">and lighten the sad cares of mind. <milestone unit="alt_poem_line" n="2a_0"/><gap reason="lost" rend=" * * * "/><note resp="perseus">Lines 10a ff are numbered as poem 2a in some editions.</note> This was as pleasing to me as the golden apple was to the fleet footed girl, which unloosed her girdle long-time fastened.</l>

notes: Lines 10a ff are numbered as poem 2a in some editions.

lines.text: O mourn, you Loves and Cupids, and all men of gracious mind. Dead is the sparrow of my girl, sparrow, darling of my girl,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:3" n="1">O mourn, you Loves and Cupids, and all men of gracious mind. Dead is the sparrow of my girl, sparrow, darling of my girl,</l>

lines.text: which she loved more than her eyes; for it was sweet as honey, and its mistress knew it as well as a girl knows her own mother. Nor did it move from her lap, but hopping round first one side then the other,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:3" n="5">which she loved more than her eyes; for it was sweet as honey, and its mistress knew it as well as a girl knows her own mother. Nor did it move from her lap, but hopping round first one side then the other,</l>

lines.text: to its mistress alone it continually chirped. Now it fares along that path of shadows from where nothing may ever return. May evil befall you, savage glooms of Orcus, which swallow up all things of fairness:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:3" n="10">to its mistress alone it continually chirped. Now it fares along that path of shadows from where nothing may ever return. May evil befall you, savage glooms of Orcus, which swallow up all things of fairness:</l>

lines.text: which have snatched away from me the comely sparrow. O wretched deed! O hapless sparrow! Now on your account my girl’s sweet eyes, swollen, redden with tear-drops.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:3" n="15">which have snatched away from me the comely sparrow. O wretched deed! O hapless sparrow! Now on your account my girl’s sweet eyes, swollen, redden with tear-drops.</l>

lines.text: That pinnace which you see, my friends, says that it was the speediest of boats, that it could gain the lead of any craft skimming the surface,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:4" n="1">That pinnace which you see, my friends, says that it was the speediest of boats, that it could gain the lead of any craft skimming the surface, </l>

lines.text: whether the task were to fly with oarblades or sail. And she denies that the shore of the menacing Adriatic denies this, or the Cyclades awkward [to navigate], or noble Rhodes and bristling Thracian Propontis, or the frim Pontic gulf,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:4" n="5">whether the task were to fly with oarblades or sail. And she denies that the shore of the menacing Adriatic denies this, or the <placeName key="tgn,7011270">Cyclades</placeName> awkward [to navigate], or noble <placeName key="tgn,7011266">Rhodes</placeName> and bristling Thracian Propontis, or the frim Pontic gulf, </l>

lines.text: where she afterwards was a pinnace, beforehand was bearded forest; and often on Cytorus’ ridge she gave out a rustling with speaking foliage. And you, Pontic Amastris, and to boxwood bearing Cytorus, the pinnace declares that this was and is most well-known to you;
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:4" n="10">where she afterwards was a pinnace, beforehand was bearded forest; and often on Cytorus’ ridge she gave out a rustling with speaking foliage. And you, Pontic Amastris, and to boxwood bearing Cytorus, the pinnace declares that this was and is most well-known to you; </l>

lines.text: she says that from its origin it stood upon your topmost peak, dipped its oars in your waters, and bore its master from there through so many seas lacking self-control, whether the wind called from port or starboard
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:4" n="15">she says that from its origin it stood upon your topmost peak, dipped its oars in your waters, and bore its master from there through so many seas lacking self-control, whether the wind called from port or starboard</l>

lines.text: or whether favorable Jove fell on both the sheets at once; and nor were any vows [from stress of storm] made be her to shore-gods, when she came from the most distant sea to this glassy lake.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:4" n="20">or whether favorable Jove fell on both the sheets at once; and nor were any vows [from stress of storm] made be her to shore-gods, when she came from the most distant sea to this glassy lake.</l>

lines.text: But these things were of before: now laid away, she grows old in peace and dedicates herself to you, twin Castor, and to Castor’s twin.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:4" n="25">But these things were of before: now laid away, she grows old in peace and dedicates herself to you, twin Castor, and to Castor’s twin.</l>

lines.text: Let us live, my Lesbia, and let us love, and count all the mumblings of sour age at a penny’s fee. Suns can set and rise again:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:5" n="1">Let us live, my Lesbia, and let us love, and count all the mumblings of sour age at a penny’s fee. Suns can set and rise again:</l>

lines.text: we when once our brief light has set must sleep through a perpetual night. Give me a thousand kisses, and then a hundred, then another thousand, then a second hundred, then another thousand without resting, then a hundred.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:5" n="5">we when once our brief light has set must sleep through a perpetual night. Give me a thousand kisses, and then a hundred, then another thousand, then a second hundred, then another thousand without resting, then a hundred.</l>

lines.text: Then, when we have made many thousands, we will confuse the count lest we know the numbering, so that no one can cast an evil eye on us through knowing the number of our kisses.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:5" n="10">Then, when we have made many thousands, we will confuse the count lest we know the numbering, so that no one can cast an evil eye on us through knowing the number of our kisses.</l>

lines.text: Flavius, you would speak of your sweetheart to Catullus, and you could not keep silent, were she not both ill-mannered and ungraceful. In truth you affect I know not what hot-blooded
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:6" n="1">Flavius, you would speak of your sweetheart to Catullus, and you could not keep silent, were she not both ill-mannered and ungraceful. In truth you affect I know not what hot-blooded</l>

lines.text: whore you love: this you are ashamed to confess. For your couch, fragrant with garlands and Syrian unguent, in no way mute cries out that you do not lie alone at night, and also the pillow and bolsters indented here and there,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:6" n="5">whore you love: this you are ashamed to confess. For your couch, fragrant with garlands and Syrian unguent, in no way mute cries out that you do not lie alone at night, and also the pillow and bolsters indented here and there,</l>

lines.text: and the creakings and joggings of the quivering bed: unless you can silence these, nothing and again nothing avails you to hide your affairs. And why? You would not display such love-weary loins unless occupied in some tomfoolery.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:6" n="10">and the creakings and joggings of the quivering bed: unless you can silence these, nothing and again nothing avails you to hide your affairs. And why? You would not display such love-weary loins unless occupied in some tomfoolery.</l>

lines.text: Therefore, whatever you have for good or ill, tell us! I want to call you and your loves to heaven in charming verse.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:6" n="15">Therefore, whatever you have for good or ill, tell us! I want to call you and your loves to heaven in charming verse.</l>

lines.text: You ask, how many kisses of yours, Lesbia, may be enough and to spare for me. As the countless Libyan sands which strew asafoetida-bearing Cyrene
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:7" n="1">You ask, how many kisses of yours, Lesbia, may be enough and to spare for me. As the countless Libyan sands which strew asafoetida-bearing <placeName key="tgn,7000639">Cyrene</placeName></l>

lines.text: between the oracle of sweltering Jove and the sacred tomb of ancient Battus, or as the many stars, when night is silent, look upon the furtive loves of mortals, to kiss you with kisses of so great a number
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:7" n="5"> between the oracle of sweltering Jove and the sacred tomb of ancient Battus, or as the many stars, when night is silent, look upon the furtive loves of mortals, to kiss you with kisses of so great a number</l>

lines.text: is enough and to spare for passion-driven Catullus: so many that prying eyes may not avail to number, nor ill tongues to bewitch.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:7" n="10">is enough and to spare for passion-driven Catullus: so many that prying eyes may not avail to number, nor ill tongues to bewitch.</l>

lines.text: Unhappy Catullus, cease your trifling and what you see lost, know to be lost. Once bright days used to shine on you when you used to go wherever your girl led you,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:8" n="1">Unhappy Catullus, cease your trifling and what you see lost, know to be lost. Once bright days used to shine on you when you used to go wherever your girl led you,</l>

lines.text: loved by us as never a girl will ever be loved. There those many joys occured which you did wish, nor was the girl unwilling. In truth bright days used once to shine on you. Now she no longer wants you: you too, powerless to avail, must not want her,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:8" n="5">loved by us as never a girl will ever be loved. There those many joys occured which you did wish, nor was the girl unwilling. In truth bright days used once to shine on you. Now she no longer wants you: you too, powerless to avail, must not want her,</l>

lines.text: do not pursue her retreating, do not live unhappy, but with firm-set mind endure, harden yourself. Farewell, girl! now Catullus hardens himself, he will not seek you, will not ask you since you are unwilling. But you will be pained, when you are not asked.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:8" n="10">do not pursue her retreating, do not live unhappy, but with firm-set mind endure, harden yourself. Farewell, girl! now Catullus hardens himself, he will not seek you, will not ask you since you are unwilling. But you will be pained, when you are not asked.</l>

lines.text: Faithless, go your way! what manner of life remains to you? who now will visit you? who find you beautiful? whom will you love now? whose will you be called? whom will you kiss? whose lips will you bite? But you, Catullus, remain firm in your hardness.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:8" n="15">Faithless, go your way! what manner of life remains to you? who now will visit you? who find you beautiful? whom will you love now? whose will you be called? whom will you kiss? whose lips will you bite? But you, Catullus, remain firm in your hardness.</l>

lines.text: Veranius, standing in the front of all my friends, had I three hundred thousand of them, have you come home to your Penates, your longing brothers and your aged mother?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:9" n="1">Veranius, standing in the front of all my friends, had I three hundred thousand of them, have you come home to your Penates, your longing brothers and your aged mother?</l>

lines.text: You have come back. O joyful news to me! I’ll see you safe and sound, and hear you speak of regions, deeds, and peoples Iberian, as is your manner; and reclining over your neck shall kiss your laughing mouth and eyes.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:9" n="5">You have come back. O joyful news to me! I’ll see you safe and sound, and hear you speak of regions, deeds, and peoples Iberian, as is your manner; and reclining over your neck shall kiss your laughing mouth and eyes.</l>

lines.text: Of all men most full of bliss, who is more happy or more blissful than I?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:9" n="10">Of all men most full of bliss, who is more happy or more blissful than I?</l>

lines.text: Varus drew me off from the Forum where I was passing the time to see his lover: a professional, as it seemed to me at first sight, neither inelegant nor lacking good looks.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:10" n="1">Varus drew me off from the Forum where I was passing the time to see his lover: a professional, as it seemed to me at first sight, neither inelegant nor lacking good looks.</l>

lines.text: When we came in, we fell to discussing various subjects, among which, how was Bithynia now, how things had gone there, and whether I had made any money there. I replied what was true, that neither ourselves
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:10" n="5">When we came in, we fell to discussing various subjects, among which, how was <placeName key="tgn,7016608">Bithynia</placeName> now, how things had gone there, and whether I had made any money there. I replied what was true, that neither ourselves</l>

lines.text: nor the praetors nor their company had brought away anything whereby to flaunt a better-scented hair-do, especially as our praetor, who boned us all, didn’t care a hair for his company. But surely, she said, you got some men to bear your litter,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:10" n="10">nor the praetors nor their company had brought away anything whereby to flaunt a better-scented hair-do, especially as our praetor, who boned us all, didn’t care a hair for his company. <q rend="double">But surely,</q> she said, <q rend="double">you got some men to bear your litter,</q></l>

lines.text: for they are said to grow there? I, to make myself appear to the girl as one of the fortunate, No, I say, it did not go that badly with me, ill as the province turned out,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:10" n="15"><q rend="double; merge">for they are said to grow there?</q> I, to make myself appear to the girl as one of the fortunate, <q rend="double">No,</q> I say, <q rend="double">it did not go that badly with me, ill as the province turned out,</q></l>

lines.text: that I could not procure eight strapping men to bear me. (But not a single one was mine either here or there who could hoist on his neck the fractured foot of my old bedstead). And she, like the saucy tramp she was,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:10" n="20"><q rend="double; merge">that I could not procure eight strapping men to bear me.</q> (But not a single one was mine either here or there who could hoist on his neck the fractured foot of my old bedstead). And she, like the saucy tramp she was,</l>

lines.text: Marrucinius Asinius, you do not use your left hand nicely amid the jests and wine: you make off with the napkins of the careless. Do you think this is witty? It escapes you, fool,

lines.text: how coarse a thing and unbecoming it is! Don’t you believe me? Believe your brother Pollio who would willingly give a talent to divert you from your thefts: for he is a lad skilled in pleasantries and clever talk.

lines.text: Therefore, either expect three hundred hendecasyllables, or return me my napkin which I esteem, not for its value but as a pledge of remembrance from my comrade.

lines.text: For Fabullus and Veranius sent me napkins as a gift from Iberian Saetabis; these I must love even as I do Veraniolus and Fabullus.

lines.text: You will feast well with me, my Fabullus, in a few days, if the gods favour you, provided you bring here with you a good and great feast, not forgetting a radiant girl

lines.text: Aurelius, father of hunger, in ages past in time now present and in future years yet to come, you long to make my lover your boy.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:21" n="1">Aurelius, father of hunger, in ages past in time now present and in future years yet to come, you long to make my lover your boy.</l>

lines.text: And you do not operate secretly: for you are with him, you joke together, closely sticking at his side you try every means. In vain: for, though you plot against me, I’ll tag you first with a boning.— Now if you were satisfied, I would be silent:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:21" n="5">And you do not operate secretly: for you are with him, you joke together, closely sticking at his side you try every means. In vain: for, though you plot against me, I’ll tag you first with a boning.— Now if you were satisfied, I would be silent:</l>

lines.text: but what irks me is that my boy, ah me! must learn to starve and thirst with you. Therefore, desist, while you may with modesty, lest you reach the end,—but by being boned.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:21" n="10">but what irks me is that my boy, ah me! must learn to starve and thirst with you. Therefore, desist, while you may with modesty, lest you reach the end,—but by being boned.</l>

lines.text: That Suffenus, Varus, whom you know well, is a man fair spoken, witty and urbane, and one who makes lengthy verses. I think he has written at full length ten thousand or more,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:22" n="1">That Suffenus, Varus, whom you know well, is a man fair spoken, witty and urbane, and one who makes lengthy verses. I think he has written at full length ten thousand or more,</l>

lines.text: nor are they set down, as commonly, on scraped parchment: regal paper, new boards, new bosses, straps, red parchment, the whole thing ruled with the lead and smoothed off with the pumice. But when you read these, that refined and urbane
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:22" n="5">nor are they set down, as commonly, on scraped parchment: regal paper, new boards, new bosses, straps, red parchment, the whole thing ruled with the lead and smoothed off with the pumice. But when you read these, that refined and urbane</l>

lines.text: Suffenus seems on the contrary to be a mere goatherd or ditch-digger, so great and shocking is the change. What can we think of this? The same man, who just now seemed a man-about-town, or if anything could be more polished than that, is stupider than the stupid countryside
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:22" n="10">Suffenus seems on the contrary to be a mere goatherd or ditch-digger, so great and shocking is the change. What can we think of this? The same man, who just now seemed a man-about-town, or if anything could be more polished than that, is stupider than the stupid countryside</l>

lines.text: as soon as he touches poetry, and nor is the same man ever as happy as when he is writing poetry—so greatly is he pleased with himself, so much does he admire himself. Still, we are all the same and are deceived, nor is there any man in whom you can not see a Suffenus in some one point.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:22" n="15">as soon as he touches poetry, and nor is the same man ever as happy as when he is writing poetry—so greatly is he pleased with himself, so much does he admire himself. Still, we are all the same and are deceived, nor is there any man in whom you can not see a Suffenus in some one point.</l>

lines.text: Each of us has his assigned delusion: but we see not what’s in the wallet on our back.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:22" n="20">Each of us has his assigned delusion: but we see not what’s in the wallet on our back.</l>

lines.text: Furius, you who have neither a slave, nor a coffer, nor a bug, nor a spider, nor fire, but have both a father and a step-mother whose teeth can munch up even flints,—
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:23" n="1">Furius, you who have neither a slave, nor a coffer, nor a bug, nor a spider, nor fire, but have both a father and a step-mother whose teeth can munch up even flints,—</l>

lines.text: you live finely with your father, and with your father’s wooden spouse. And no wonder: for you are all in good health, finely you digest, you fear nothing, not arson, not the fall of your house,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:23" n="5">you live finely with your father, and with your father’s wooden spouse. And no wonder: for you are all in good health, finely you digest, you fear nothing, not arson, not the fall of your house,</l>

lines.text: not impious thefts, not plots of poison, no perilous happenings whatsoever. And you have bodies drier than horn (or if there is anything more arid still, if ought there be), parched by sun, frost, and famine.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:23" n="10">not impious thefts, not plots of poison, no perilous happenings whatsoever. And you have bodies drier than horn (or if there is anything more arid still, if ought there be), parched by sun, frost, and famine.</l>

lines.text: So why is it not happy and well with you? Sweat is a stranger to you, absent also are saliva, phlegm, and evil nose-snot. Add to this cleanliness the thing that’s still more cleanly, that your backside is purer than a salt-cellar,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:23" n="15">So why is it not happy and well with you? Sweat is a stranger to you, absent also are saliva, phlegm, and evil nose-snot. Add to this cleanliness the thing that’s still more cleanly, that your backside is purer than a salt-cellar,</l>

lines.text: nor do you crap ten times in the whole year, and then it is harder than beans and pebbles; and if you rub and crumble it in your hands, you can’t ever dirty a finger.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:23" n="20">nor do you crap ten times in the whole year, and then it is harder than beans and pebbles; and if you rub and crumble it in your hands, you can’t ever dirty a finger.</l>

lines.text: Spurn not these goodly gifts and favours, Furius, nor think lightly of them; and stop always begging for a hundred sesterces: for you are happy enough!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:23" n="24">Spurn not these goodly gifts and favours, Furius, nor think lightly of them; and stop always begging for a hundred sesterces: for you are happy enough!</l>

lines.text: O you who are the little flower of Juventian race, not only of these now living, but of those that were before and also of those that will be in the coming years, I’d rather that you had given the wealth of Midas
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:24" n="1">O you who are the little flower of Juventian race, not only of these now living, but of those that were before and also of those that will be in the coming years, I’d rather that you had given the wealth of Midas</l>

lines.text: to that man who owns neither a slave nor coffer, than that you should suffer yourself to be loved by him. What? you ask. Isn’t he a fine looking man? He is; but this fine looking man has neither a slave nor coffer. Slight and make light of this as you please:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:24" n="5">to that man who owns neither a slave nor coffer, than that you should suffer yourself to be loved by him. <q rend="double">What?</q> you ask. <q rend="double">Isn’t he a fine looking man?</q> He is; but this fine looking man has neither a slave nor coffer. lines.text: Thallus you sodomite, softer than rabbit’s fur, or goose’s marrow, or an ear lobe, or an old man’s drooping penis, and the cobwebs there; again Thallus greedier than the driving storm,

lines.text: lest the stinging scourge shamefully score your downy little butt and delicate little hands, and you unaccustomedly heave and toss like a tiny boat surprised on the vast sea by a raging storm.

lines.text: Furius, your little house is pitted not against the southern breeze nor the western wind nor cruel Boreas nor sunny east, but fifteen thousand two hundred sesterces.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:26" n="1">Furius, your little house is pitted not against the southern breeze nor the western wind nor cruel Boreas nor sunny east, but fifteen thousand two hundred sesterces.</l>

lines.text: O horrible and baleful wind.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:26" n="5">O horrible and baleful wind.</l>

lines.text: Boy cupbearer of old Falernian, pour me more pungent cups as bids the laws of Postumia, mistress of the feast, drunker than a drunken grape.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:27" n="1">Boy cupbearer of old Falernian, pour me more pungent cups as bids the laws of Postumia, mistress of the feast, drunker than a drunken grape.</l>

lines.text: But off with you, as far as you please, crystal waters, bane of wine, depart you to the sober: here the Thyonian juice is pure.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:27" n="5">But off with you, as far as you please, crystal waters, bane of wine, depart you to the sober: here the Thyonian juice is pure.</l>

lines.text: Piso’s Company, a penniless staff, with lightweight knapsacks, scantly packed, most dear Veranius you, and my Fabullus too, how goes it with you? Have you borne frost and famine enough with that sot?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:28" n="1">Piso’s Company, a penniless staff, with lightweight knapsacks, scantly packed, most dear Veranius you, and my Fabullus too, how goes it with you? Have you borne frost and famine enough with that sot?</l>

lines.text: Which in your tablets appear—the profits or expenses? So with me, who when I followed a praetor, inscribed more gifts than gains.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:28" n="6">Which in your tablets appear—the profits or expenses? So with me, who when I followed a praetor, inscribed more gifts than gains.</l>

lines.text: O Memmius, well and slowly did you bone me, supine, day by day, with the whole of that beam. But, from what I see, in like case you have been; for you have been crammed with no smaller a poker. Courting friends of high rank! But may the gods and goddesses heap ill upon you,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:28" n="9"><q rend="double">O Memmius, well and slowly did you bone me, supine, day by day, with the whole of that beam.</q> But, from what I see, in like case you have been; for you have been crammed with no smaller a poker. lines.text: disgraces to Romulus and Remus.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:28" n="15">disgraces to Romulus and Remus.</l>

lines.text: Who can see this, who can stand it, save the shameless, the glutton, and gambler, that Mamurra Mentula should possess what long-haired Gaul had and remotest Britain had before?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:29" n="1">Who can see this, who can stand it, save the shameless, the glutton, and gambler, that Mamurra Mentula should possess what long-haired <placeName key="tgn,1000070">Gaul</placeName> had and remotest <placeName key="tgn,7008653">Britain</placeName> had before?</l>

lines.text: You sodomite Romulus, will you see this and bear it? Then you are shameless, a glutton and a gambler. And will he now, proud and overflowing, saunter over each one’s bed, like a little white dove or an Adonis? You sodomite Romulus, will you see this and bear it?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:29" n="5">You sodomite Romulus, will you see this and bear it? You sodomite Romulus, will you see this and bear it?</l>

lines.text: Then you are shameless, a glutton and a gambler. For such a name, Generalissimo, have you been to the furthest island of the west, that this love-weary Mentula of yours should squander twenty or thirty million?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:29" n="10">Then you are shameless, a glutton and a gambler. For such a name, Generalissimo, have you been to the furthest island of the west, that this love-weary Mentula of yours should squander twenty or thirty million?</l>

lines.text: What is it but a skewed liberality? Perhaps he spent too little, or perhaps he was washed clean? First he wasted his patrimony; second the loot from Pontus; then third the loot from Spain, which even the goldbearing Tagus knows.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:29" n="15">What is it but a skewed liberality? lines.text: Now he is feared by Gauls and Britain. Why do you indulge this scoundrel? What can he do but devour well-fattened inheritances? Was it for such a name, † most wealthy father-in-law and son-in-law, that you have destroyed everything?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:29" n="20">Now he is feared by Gauls and <placeName key="tgn,7008653">Britain</placeName>. lines.text: Alfenus, unmindful and unfaithful to your comrades true, is there now no pity in you, hard of heart, for your sweet loving friend? Do you betray me now, and not hesitate to play me false now, dishonourable one? Yet the irreverent deeds of traitorous men do not please the dwellers in heaven:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:30" n="1">Alfenus, unmindful and unfaithful to your comrades true, is there now no pity in you, hard of heart, for your sweet loving friend? Do you betray me now, and not hesitate to play me false now, dishonourable one? Yet the irreverent deeds of traitorous men do not please the dwellers in heaven:</l>

lines.text: this you take no heed of, leaving me wretched among my ills. Tell me, ah, what may men do, or in whom may they have their trust? Surely you used to bid me entrust my soul to you, unfair, drawing my affections to yourself, as though all were safely mine. Yet now you withdraw yourself, and all your purposeless words and deeds
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:30" n="5">this you take no heed of, leaving me wretched among my ills. Yet now you withdraw yourself, and all your purposeless words and deeds</l>

lines.text: you suffer the winds and airy clouds to bear away. If you have forgotten, yet the gods remember, Faith remembers, and in time to come will make you regret your doing.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:30" n="10">you suffer the winds and airy clouds to bear away. If you have forgotten, yet the gods remember, Faith remembers, and in time to come will make you regret your doing.</l>

lines.text: Sirmio! Eyelet of islands and peninsulas, which each Neptune holds whether in limpid lakes or on the wide sea, how gladly and how happily do I see you again,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:31" n="1"><placeName key="tgn,7005771">Sirmio</placeName>! Eyelet of islands and peninsulas, which each Neptune holds whether in limpid lakes or on the wide sea, how gladly and how happily do I see you again,</l>

lines.text: scarcely believing that I’ve left behind Thynia and the Bithynian plains, and that I gaze on you safe and sound. O what greater blessing than cares released, when the mind casts down its burden, and when wearied with the toil of travel we reach our hearth,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:31" n="5">scarcely believing that I’ve left behind Thynia and the Bithynian plains, and that I gaze on you safe and sound. O what greater blessing than cares released, when the mind casts down its burden, and when wearied with the toil of travel we reach our hearth,</l>

lines.text: and rest in the long-for bed. This and only this repays our numerous labors. Hail, lovely Sirmio, and rejoice in your master; and rejoice, you waves of the Lybian lake; laugh, you laughters echoing from my home.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:31" n="10">and rest in the long-for bed. This and only this repays our numerous labors. Hail, lovely <placeName key="tgn,7005771">Sirmio</placeName>, and rejoice in your master; and rejoice, you waves of the Lybian lake; laugh, you laughters echoing from my home.</l>

lines.text: Please, my sweet Ipsithilla, my delight, my charmer: order me to come to you at noon. And if you should order this, it will be useful
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:32" n="1">Please, my sweet Ipsithilla, my delight, my charmer: order me to come to you at noon. And if you should order this, it will be useful</l>

lines.text: if no one makes fast the outer door [against me], and don’t be minded to go out, but stay at home and prepare for us nine continuous love-makings. In truth if you are minded, give the order at once:

lines.text: O best of the thieves of the baths, Vibennius the father, and his sexually submissive son (for the father is the filthier with the right hand, the son is the greedier with the backside),

lines.text: We, upright maids and youths, are in Diana’s care: upright youths and maids, we sing Diana.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:34" n="1">We, upright maids and youths, are in Diana’s care: upright youths and maids, we sing Diana.</l>

lines.text: O Latonia, progeny great of greatest Jove, whom your mother bore beneath Delian olive, that you might be queen of lofty mounts,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:34" n="5">O Latonia, progeny great of greatest Jove, whom your mother bore beneath Delian olive, that you might be queen of lofty mounts,</l>

lines.text: of foliaged groves, of remote glens, and of winding streams. You are called Juno Lucina by the mother in the pangs of childbirth,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:34" n="10">of foliaged groves, of remote glens, and of winding streams. You are called Juno Lucina by the mother in the pangs of childbirth,</l>

lines.text: you are named potent Trivia and Luna with an ill-got light. You, Goddess, with monthly march measuring the yearly course, glut with produce the rustic roofs of the farmer.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:34" n="15">you are named potent Trivia and <persName><surname>Luna</surname></persName> with an ill-got light. You, Goddess, with monthly march measuring the yearly course, glut with produce the rustic roofs of the farmer.</l>

lines.text: Be you hallowed by whatever name you prefer; and cherish, with your good aid, as you are accustomed, the ancient race of Romulus.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:34" n="21">Be you hallowed by whatever name you prefer; and cherish, with your good aid, as you are accustomed, the ancient race of Romulus.</l>

lines.text: Paper, I would like you say to that sweet poet, my comrade, Caecilius, that he come to Verona, quitting New Comum’s city-walls and Larius’ shore;
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:35" n="1">Paper, I would like you say to that sweet poet, my comrade, Caecilius, that he come to <placeName key="perseus,Verona">Verona</placeName>, quitting New Comum’s city-walls and Larius’ shore;</l>

lines.text: for I want him to receive certain thoughts from a friend of his and mine. Therefore, if he is wise, he’ll devour the way, although a bright-hued girl a thousand times calls him back when he goes,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:35" n="5">for I want him to receive certain thoughts from a friend of his and mine. Therefore, if he is wise, he’ll devour the way, although a bright-hued girl a thousand times calls him back when he goes,</l>

lines.text: and flinging both arms around his neck asks him to delay—she who now, if truth is reported to me, is undone with immoderate love of him. For, since the time she read the beginning of his Mistress of Dindymus,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:35" n="10">and flinging both arms around his neck asks him to delay—she who now, if truth is reported to me, is undone with immoderate love of him. lines.text: flames have been devouring the innermost marrow of the poor little girl. I forgive you, girl, more learned than the Sapphic muse: for charmingly has the Great Mother been begun by Caecilius.
