lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:37" n="10">I’ll scrawl dirty pictures all over the front of your tavern. For my girl, who has fled from my embrace, she whom I loved as none will be loved, for whom I fought fierce fights, has seated herself here. All of you, good men and rich,</l>

lines.text: and also, (O cursed shame) all of you piddling back-alley fornicators, are making love to her; and you above all, Egnatius, one of the long-haired race, the son of Celtiberia full of rabbits, whose quality is stamped by dense-grown beard,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:37" n="15">and also, (O cursed shame) all of you piddling back-alley fornicators, are making love to her; and you above all, Egnatius, one of the long-haired race, the son of Celtiberia full of rabbits, whose quality is stamped by dense-grown beard,</l>

lines.text: and teeth scrubbed with Spanish urine.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:37" n="20"> and teeth scrubbed with Spanish urine.</l>

lines.text: It is ill, Cornificius, with your Catullus, it is ill, by Hercules, and most unbearably; and greater, greater ill, each day and hour!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:38" n="1">It is ill, Cornificius, with your Catullus, it is ill, by Hercules, and most unbearably; and greater, greater ill, each day and hour!</l>

lines.text: And you, what solace do you give, even the tiniest, the lightest, by your words? I’m angry with you. Is my love worth this? Yet one little message would cheer me, though more full of sadness than the tears of Simonides.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:38" n="4">And you, what solace do you give, even the tiniest, the lightest, by your words? I’m angry with you. Is my love worth this? Yet one little message would cheer me, though more full of sadness than the tears of Simonides.</l>

lines.text: Egnatius, who has shiny, white teeth, grins forever everywhere. If he is in court, when counsel excites tears, he grins. If he be at funeral pyre where one mourns a son devoted,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:39" n="1">Egnatius, who has shiny, white teeth, grins forever everywhere. If he is in court, when counsel excites tears, he grins. If he be at funeral pyre where one mourns a son devoted,</l>

lines.text: where a bereft mother’s tears stream for her only son, he grins. Whatever it may be, wherever he is, whatever may happen, he grins. Such an ill habit has he—neither in good taste, I suppose, nor refined. Therefore take note from me, my good Egnatius.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:39" n="5">where a bereft mother’s tears stream for her only son, he grins. Whatever it may be, wherever he is, whatever may happen, he grins. Such an ill habit has he—neither in good taste, I suppose, nor refined. Therefore take note from me, my good Egnatius.</l>

lines.text: Whether you are from the city or Sabine or Tiburtine, or a thrifty Umbrian or a fat Etruscan, or a dark, toothy Lanuvian, or Transpadine (to touch upon my own folk also), or whoever of those who cleanly wash their teeth,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:39" n="10">Whether you are from the city or <placeName key="tgn,7021127">Sabine</placeName> or Tiburtine, or a thrifty Umbrian or a fat Etruscan, or a dark, toothy Lanuvian, or Transpadine (to touch upon my own folk also), or whoever of those who cleanly wash their teeth,</l>

lines.text: still I wish you wouldn’t grin forever everywhere; for nothing is more senseless than senseless giggling. Now you’re a Celtiberian: and in the Celtiberian land early in the morning they piss and scrub their teeth and pinky gums with it,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:39" n="15">still I wish you wouldn’t grin forever everywhere; for nothing is more senseless than senseless giggling. Now you’re a Celtiberian: and in the Celtiberian land early in the morning they piss and scrub their teeth and pinky gums with it,</l>

lines.text: so that the higher the polish on your teeth, the more it proclaims that you have drunk your piss.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:39" n="20">so that the higher the polish on your teeth, the more it proclaims that you have drunk your piss.</l>

lines.text: What ill-set mind, poor little Ravidus, thrusts you headlong at my iambics? What god, none advocate of good for you, stirs you to a senseless quarrel?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:40" n="1">What ill-set mind, poor little Ravidus, thrusts you headlong at my iambics? What god, none advocate of good for you, stirs you to a senseless quarrel?</l>

lines.text: That you may be in the people’s mouth? What do you want? Do you want to be famous, no matter in what way? You will be, but by our long-drawn vengeance, since you wanted to love my lover.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:40" n="5">That you may be in the people’s mouth? What do you want? Do you want to be famous, no matter in what way? You will be, but by our long-drawn vengeance, since you wanted to love my lover.</l>

lines.text: Ameana, a love-worn girl, asks me for a whole ten thousand, that girl with an ugly little nose, wench of the bankrupt Formian.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:41" n="1">Ameana, a love-worn girl, asks me for a whole ten thousand, that girl with an ugly little nose, wench of the bankrupt Formian.</l>

lines.text: You near of kin in whose care the girl is, summon both friends and doctors: for the girl is not sane, and is not accustomed to ask her mirror how she looks.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:41" n="5">You near of kin in whose care the girl is, summon both friends and doctors: for the girl is not sane, and is not accustomed to ask her mirror how she looks.</l>

lines.text: O come, all ye hendecasyllables, as many as you are, from every part, all of you, as many soever as you be! A filthy whore thinks that I am a joke, and says she won’t return to me your
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:42" n="1">O come, all ye hendecasyllables, as many as you are, from every part, all of you, as many soever as you be! A filthy whore thinks that I am a joke, and says she won’t return to me your</l>

lines.text: writing tablets, if you can stand it. Let’s pursue her, and claim them back. Who is she? you ask. That one, whom you see strutting disgracefully, grinning with annoyance like a mime with a face like a Gallic puppy.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:42" n="5"> writing tablets, if you can stand it. Let’s pursue her, and claim them back. <q rend="double">Who is she?</q> you ask. That one, whom you see strutting disgracefully, grinning with annoyance like a mime with a face like a Gallic puppy.</l>

lines.text: Surround her, and claim them back. Filthy whore, give back the writing tablets; give back, filthy whore, the writing tablets. You don’t give two cents? You slime, you whorehouse, or if you could be anything even more loathsome!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:42" n="10">Surround her, and claim them back. <q rend="double">Filthy whore, give back the writing tablets; give back, filthy whore, the writing tablets.</q> You don’t give two cents? You slime, you whorehouse, or if you could be anything even more loathsome!</l>

lines.text: But you mustn’t think that this is enough. For if nothing else we can extort a blush on your brazened bitch’s face. We’ll yell again in heightened voice, Filthy whore, give back the writing tablets;
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:42" n="15">But you mustn’t think that this is enough. For if nothing else we can extort a blush on your brazened bitch’s face. We’ll yell again in heightened voice, <q rend="double">Filthy whore, give back the writing tablets;</q></l>

lines.text: give back, filthy whore, the writing tablets. But we do no good, she isn’t moved. We must change our approach and our tune, if you can make further progress—Chaste and honest, give back our writing tablets.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:42" n="20"><q rend="double; merge">give back, filthy whore, the writing tablets.</q> But we do no good, she isn’t moved. We must change our approach and our tune, if you can make further progress—<q rend="double">Chaste and honest, give back our writing tablets.</q></l>

lines.text: Hail, girl with nose not the smallest, and with foot not lovely, and with eyes not black, and with fingers not long, and with mouth not dry and with tongue not so very elegant,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:43" n="1">Hail, girl with nose not the smallest, and with foot not lovely, and with eyes not black, and with fingers not long, and with mouth not dry and with tongue not so very elegant,</l>

lines.text: the wench of the bankrupt Formian. And the province declares you to be lovely? With you our Lesbia is to be compared? O generation witless and unmannerly!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:43" n="5">the wench of the bankrupt Formian. And the province declares you to be lovely? With you our Lesbia is to be compared? O generation witless and unmannerly!</l>

lines.text: O, Homestead of ours, whether Sabine or Tiburtine (for people in whose heart it is not to wound Catullus declare you Tiburtine, but those in whose heart it is, will wager anything you’re Sabine)
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:44" n="1">O, Homestead of ours, whether <placeName key="tgn,7021127">Sabine</placeName> or Tiburtine (for people in whose heart it is not to wound Catullus declare you Tiburtine, but those in whose heart it is, will wager anything you’re <placeName key="tgn,7021127">Sabine</placeName>)</l>

lines.text: but whether Sabine or more truly Tiburtine, I was glad to be within your rural country-home, and to cast off an ill cough from my chest, which—not unearned—my belly granted me, for grasping after luxurious meals.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:44" n="5">but whether <placeName key="tgn,7021127">Sabine</placeName> or more truly Tiburtine, I was glad to be within your rural country-home, and to cast off an ill cough from my chest, which—not unearned—my belly granted me, for grasping after luxurious meals.</l>

lines.text: For, while I want to be Sestius’ guest, I read his defence against the plaintiff Antius, crammed with venom and pestilence. Hence a chill heavy rheum and fitful cough shook me continually until I fled to your asylum,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:44" n="10">For, while I want to be Sestius’ guest, I read his defence against the plaintiff Antius, crammed with venom and pestilence. Hence a chill heavy rheum and fitful cough shook me continually until I fled to your asylum,</l>

lines.text: and brought me back to health with rest and nettle-broth. Therefore, refreshed, I give you utmost thanks, that you have not avenged my fault. Nor do I pray now for anything but that, if I should retake Sestius’ abominable script,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:44" n="15">and brought me back to health with rest and nettle-broth. Therefore, refreshed, I give you utmost thanks, that you have not avenged my fault. Nor do I pray now for anything but that, if I should retake Sestius’ abominable script,</l>

lines.text: its chill may bring a cold and cough to Sestius himself; and he invites me [to dinner] whenever I read one of his bad books.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:44" n="20">its chill may bring a cold and cough to Sestius himself; and he invites me [to dinner] whenever I read one of his bad books.</l>

lines.text: Septimius, holding his lover Acme in his lap, says, My Acme, if I do not love you to death, and am not prepared to love you constantly all the years in time to come,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:45" n="1">Septimius, holding his lover Acme in his lap, says, <q rend="double">My Acme, if I do not love you to death, and am not prepared to love you constantly all the years in time to come,</q></l>

lines.text: as much and the most as one can who is desperately in love—alone in Libya or in torrid India may I come face to face with a grey-eyed lion. When he said this, Love, leftwards as before, with approbation rightwards sneezed.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:45" n="5"><q rend="double; merge">as much and the most as one can who is desperately in love—alone in <placeName key="tgn,1000172">Libya</placeName> or in torrid <placeName key="tgn,7000198">India</placeName> may I come face to face with a grey-eyed lion.</q> When he said this, Love, leftwards as before, with approbation rightwards sneezed.</l>

lines.text: Then Acme slightly bending back her head, and kissed the intoxicated eyes of her sweet boy with her rose-red lips. So, she said, my life, Septimillus, we shall serve this lord alone from now on,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:45" n="10">Then Acme slightly bending back her head, and kissed the intoxicated eyes of her sweet boy with her rose-red lips. <q rend="double">So,</q> she said, <q rend="double">my life, Septimillus, we shall serve this lord alone from now on,</q></l>

lines.text: as greater, keener fire burns the more amid my soft marrow. When she said this, Love, leftwards as before, with approbation rightwards sneezed. Now made complete under good auspices,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:45" n="15"><q rend="double; merge">as greater, keener fire burns the more amid my soft marrow.</q> When she said this, Love, leftwards as before, with approbation rightwards sneezed. Now made complete under good auspices,</l>

lines.text: with mutual minds they love and are loved. Poor little Septimius wants Acme alone more than [the wealth of] the Syria or Britain: in Septimius alone the faithful Acme takes delight and pleasure.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:45" n="20">with mutual minds they love and are loved. Poor little Septimius wants Acme alone more than [the wealth of] the <placeName key="tgn,1000140">Syria</placeName> or <placeName key="tgn,7008653">Britain</placeName>: in Septimius alone the faithful Acme takes delight and pleasure.</l>

lines.text: Whoever has seen happier people, whoever a more propitious Love?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:45" n="25">Whoever has seen happier people, whoever a more propitious Love?</l>

lines.text: Now spring brings back mild breezes without cold, now heaven’s equinoctial fury falls silent at Zephyr’s pleasant breezes. Let the Phrygian meadows be left behind, Catullus,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:46" n="1">Now spring brings back mild breezes without cold, now heaven’s equinoctial fury falls silent at Zephyr’s pleasant breezes. Let the Phrygian meadows be left behind, Catullus,</l>

lines.text: and the teeming fields of sun-scorched Nicaea: let us fly to the glorious cities of Asia. Now my palpitating soul longs to wander, now happy in their zeal my feet grow strong. O sweet band of comrades, fare you well,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:46" n="5">and the teeming fields of sun-scorched <placeName key="tgn,7008773">Nicaea</placeName>: let us fly to the glorious cities of <placeName key="tgn,1000004">Asia</placeName>. Now my palpitating soul longs to wander, now happy in their zeal my feet grow strong. O sweet band of comrades, fare you well,</l>

lines.text: whom various roads in different directions carry back all at once setting out far from home.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:46" n="10">whom various roads in different directions carry back all at once setting out far from home.</l>

lines.text: Porcius and Socration, the two left hands of Piso, scurf and hunger of the world, has that verpus Priapus placed you before my Veraniolus and Fabullus?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:47" n="1">Porcius and Socration, the two left hands of Piso, scurf and hunger of the world, has that verpus Priapus placed you before my Veraniolus and Fabullus?</l>

lines.text: Do you spend the day luxuriously in expensive feasts? Do my comrades seek out dinner invitations the cross-roads?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:47" n="5">Do you spend the day luxuriously in expensive feasts? Do my comrades seek out dinner invitations the cross-roads?</l>

lines.text: If someone let me kiss continually your honey-sweet eyes, Juventius, continually I’d kiss even to three hundred thousand kisses, nor ever should I seem on the verge of having enough,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:48" n="1">If someone let me kiss continually your honey-sweet eyes, Juventius, continually I’d kiss even to three hundred thousand kisses, nor ever should I seem on the verge of having enough,</l>

lines.text: not even if the crop of our kisses should be thicker than dried wheat sheaves.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:48" n="5">not even if the crop of our kisses should be thicker than dried wheat sheaves.</l>

lines.text: Most eloquent of Romulus’ descendancy—as many as there are, who have been, O Marcus Tullius, and who will be after in other years—to you Catullus gives his greatest gratitude,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:49" n="1">Most eloquent of Romulus’ descendancy—as many as there are, who have been, O Marcus Tullius, and who will be after in other years—to you Catullus gives his greatest gratitude,</l>

lines.text: the worst poet of all by as much as you are the best advocate of all.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:49" n="5">the worst poet of all by as much as you are the best advocate of all.</l>

lines.text: Yesterday, Licinius, in leisure much we played upon my tablets, as became us, men of fancy. Each jotting verses in turn
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:50" n="1">Yesterday, Licinius, in leisure much we played upon my tablets, as became us, men of fancy. Each jotting verses in turn</l>

lines.text: played first in this meter then in that, exchanging mutual epigrams amid jokes and wine. But I departed from there, afire, Licinius, with your wit and charm, so that food was useless to my wretched self;
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:50" n="5">played first in this meter then in that, exchanging mutual epigrams amid jokes and wine. But I departed from there, afire, Licinius, with your wit and charm, so that food was useless to my wretched self;</l>

lines.text: nor could sleep close my eyes in quiet, but all over the bed in restless fury did I toss, longing to behold daylight that I might speak with you, and again we might be together. But afterwards, when my limbs, weakened by my restless labours,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:50" n="10">nor could sleep close my eyes in quiet, but all over the bed in restless fury did I toss, longing to behold daylight that I might speak with you, and again we might be together. But afterwards, when my limbs, weakened by my restless labours,</l>

lines.text: lay stretched in semi-death upon the bed, I made this poem for you, my delight, from which you will perceive my pain. Now beware of presumptuousness, and beware of rejecting our pleadings, I pray you, apple of my eye,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:50" n="15">lay stretched in semi-death upon the bed, I made this poem for you, my delight, from which you will perceive my pain. Now beware of presumptuousness, and beware of rejecting our pleadings, I pray you, apple of my eye,</l>

lines.text: lest Nemesis exact her dues from you. She is a forceful Goddess; beware her wrath.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:50" n="20">lest Nemesis exact her dues from you. She is a forceful Goddess; beware her wrath.</l>

lines.text: He seems to me to be equal to a god, he, if such were lawful, to surpass the gods, who sitting across from you again and again gazes on you, and listens to you
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:51" n="1">He seems to me to be equal to a god, he, if such were lawful, to surpass the gods, who sitting across from you again and again gazes on you, and listens to you</l>

lines.text: sweetly laughing, which snatches away from sombre me my every sense: for the instant I glance on you, Lesbia, nothing is left to me [of voice], but my tongue is numbed, a keen-edged
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:51" n="5">sweetly laughing, which snatches away from sombre me my every sense: for the instant I glance on you, Lesbia, nothing is left to me [of voice], but my tongue is numbed, a keen-edged</l>

lines.text: flame spreads through my limbs, with sound self-caused my twin ears sing, and my eyes are enwrapped with night.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:51" n="10">flame spreads through my limbs, with sound self-caused my twin ears sing, and my eyes are enwrapped with night.</l>

lines.text: Leisure, Catullus, to you is hurtful: in leisure beyond measure do you exult and pass your life.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:51" n="13"><milestone unit="alt_poem_line" n="51b_14"/>Leisure, Catullus, to you is hurtful: in leisure beyond measure do you exult and pass your life.<note resp="perseus">Lines 13-16 are labeled as poem 51b in the print.</note></l>

lines.text: Leisure first ruined rulers and prosperous cities.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:51" n="15"><milestone unit="alt_poem_line" n="51b_16"/>Leisure first ruined rulers and prosperous cities.</l>

notes: Lines 13-16 are labeled as poem 51b in the print.

lines.text: What is it, Catullus, why delay your death? Nonius the tumor is seated in the curule chair, Vatinius lies his way to the consulship: what is it, Catullus, why delay your death?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:52" n="1">What is it, Catullus, why delay your death? Nonius the tumor is seated in the curule chair, Vatinius lies his way to the consulship: what is it, Catullus, why delay your death?</l>

lines.text: I just had to laugh at someone in the crowded court who, when with admirable art my Calvus had set forth Vatinius’ crimes, with hands uplifted in admiration thus spoke:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:53" n="1">I just had to laugh at someone in the crowded court who, when with admirable art my Calvus had set forth Vatinius’ crimes, with hands uplifted in admiration thus spoke:</l>

lines.text: Great Gods, the fluent little Salaputian!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:53" n="5"><q rend="double">Great Gods, the fluent little Salaputian!</q></l>

lines.text: Otho’s tiny little head is * * * * the master’s uncouth half-soaped legs, Libo’s light and delicate wind * * * * * if not all things I wish would displease
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:54" n="1">Otho’s tiny little head is <gap reason="lost" rend=" * * * * "/> the master’s uncouth half-soaped legs, Libo’s light and delicate wind <gap reason="lost" rend=" * * * * * "/> if not all things I wish would displease</l>

lines.text: you and Fuficius, that warmed-over old man * again you will be enraged at my undeserving iambics, Generalissimo.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:54" n="5">you and Fuficius, that warmed-over old man <gap reason="lost" rend=" * "/><note resp="perseus">Lines 6-7 (with or without a gap preceding) are labeled 54b in the print. They have been combined with poem 54 here in keeping with convention.</note> <milestone unit="alt_poem_line" n="54b_1"/>again you will be enraged at my undeserving iambics, Generalissimo.</l>

notes: Lines 6-7 (with or without a gap preceding) are labeled 54b in the print. They have been combined with poem 54 here in keeping with convention.

lines.text: We beg, if maybe it’s not too much trouble, you’ll show us where your haunt may be. We looked for you in the smaller Campus, for you in the Circus, for you in every bookshop,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:55" n="1">We beg, if maybe it’s not too much trouble, you’ll show us where your haunt may be. We looked for you in the smaller Campus, for you in the Circus, for you in every bookshop,</l>

lines.text: for you in Jupiter’s holy temple. My friend, on Magnus’ promenade I grabbed every girl I saw whose looks were unruffled, and at the same time I demanded loudly,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:55" n="5">for you in <persName><surname>Jupiter</surname></persName>’s holy temple. My friend, on Magnus’ promenade I grabbed every girl I saw whose looks were unruffled, and at the same time I demanded loudly,</l>

lines.text: Give me back Camerius, you wretched girls. One of them, drawing back her naked . . . Look! he’s hiding here between my rosey-red nipples! But bearing with you is a labor of Hercules now.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:55" n="10"><q rend="double">Give me back Camerius, you wretched girls.</q> One of them, drawing back her naked <gap reason="lost" rend=" . . . "/> <q rend="double">Look! he’s hiding here between my rosey-red nipples!</q> But bearing with you is a labor of <persName><surname>Hercules</surname></persName> now. </l>

lines.text: Not if I were molded into the Cretan guard, not if I were born with Pegasean wing,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:55" n="23">Not if I were molded into the Cretan guard, not if I were born with Pegasean wing,</l>

lines.text: or I Ladas, or Perseus with winged foot, or Rhesus’ swift and snowy team: add to these the feathery-footed and winged ones, ask at the same time the course of the winds: which bound up, Camerius, you name as mine;
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:55" n="25">or I Ladas, or Perseus with winged foot, or Rhesus’ swift and snowy team: add to these the feathery-footed and winged ones, ask at the same time the course of the winds: which bound up, Camerius, you name as mine;</l>

lines.text: yet exhausted in my every marrow and with many a faintness consumed, I would be in my quest for you, my friend.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:55" n="30">yet exhausted in my every marrow and with many a faintness consumed, I would be in my quest for you, my friend.</l>

lines.text: Do you deny that you bear yourself in such great arrogance, my friend?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:55" n="14">Do you deny that you bear yourself in such great arrogance, my friend?</l>

lines.text: Tell us where you will be, declare it boldly, give up the secret, trust it to the light. What, do the milk-white maidens detain you? If you hold your tongue closed up in your mouth, you squander Love’s every fruit:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:55" n="15">Tell us where you will be, declare it boldly, give up the secret, trust it to the light. What, do the milk-white maidens detain you? If you hold your tongue closed up in your mouth, you squander Love’s every fruit:</l>

lines.text: for Venus joys in words and talk. Yet if you wish, you may bar your palate, as long as you are a partner of true love.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:55" n="20">for <persName><surname>Venus</surname></persName> joys in words and talk. Yet if you wish, you may bar your palate, as long as you are a partner of true love.</l>

lines.text: O thing ridiculous, Cato, and funny, and worthy of your ears and of your laughter. Laugh, Cato, the more you love Catullus: the thing is ridiculous and too funny.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:56" n="1">O thing ridiculous, <persName><surname>Cato</surname></persName>, and funny, and worthy of your ears and of your laughter. Laugh, <persName><surname>Cato</surname></persName>, the more you love Catullus: the thing is ridiculous and too funny.</l>

lines.text: Just now I caught a boy a-thrusting in a girl: and, so please you, Dione, for lack of a weapon I slayed him with my own rigidity.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:56" n="5">Just now I caught a boy a-thrusting in a girl: and, so please you, Dione, for lack of a weapon I slayed him with my own rigidity.</l>

lines.text: Beautifully it fits the shameless sodomites, Mamurra and sexually submissive Caesar. It’s no wonder: they share like stains—the one from the City, the other, Formian—
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:57" n="1">Beautifully it fits the shameless sodomites, Mamurra and sexually submissive Caesar. It’s no wonder: they share like stains—the one from the City, the other, Formian—</l>

lines.text: which stay deep-marked and they can not be washed off. Debauched twins each, both learned, both in one bed, one not more than the other the greater greedier adulterer, allied rivals of the girls.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:57" n="5">which stay deep-marked and they can not be washed off. Debauched twins each, both learned, both in one bed, one not more than the other the greater greedier adulterer, allied rivals of the girls.</l>

lines.text: Beautifully it fits the shameless sodomites.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:57" n="10">Beautifully it fits the shameless sodomites.</l>

lines.text: O Caelius, our Lesbia, that Lesbia, the self-same Lesbia whom Catullus loved more than himself and all his own, now at the cross-roads and in the alleyways
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:58" n="1">O Caelius, our <persName><surname>Lesbia</surname></persName>, that <persName><surname>Lesbia</surname></persName>, the self-same Lesbia whom Catullus loved more than himself and all his own, now at the cross-roads and in the alleyways</l>

lines.text: husks off the high-spirited descendants of Remus.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:58" n="5">husks off the high-spirited descendants of <persName><surname>Remus</surname></persName>.</l>

lines.text: Rufa of Bononia blows Rufulus, she the wife of Menenius. Often you have seen her among the tombs, snatching her meal from the funeral pyre. When she chases after the bread which has rolled from the fire,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:59" n="1">Rufa of <placeName key="tgn,7010649">Bononia</placeName> blows Rufulus, she the wife of Menenius. Often you have seen her among the tombs, snatching her meal from the funeral pyre. When she chases after the bread which has rolled from the fire,</l>

lines.text: she is buffeted by the half-shaven cremator.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:59" n="5">she is buffeted by the half-shaven cremator.</l>

lines.text: Did a lioness of the Libyan mountains beget you, or Scylla yelping from her lowmost groin with mind so harsh and loathsome,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:60" n="1">Did a lioness of the Libyan mountains beget you, or Scylla yelping from her lowmost groin with mind so harsh and loathsome,</l>

lines.text: that you have contempt for a suppliant’s voice in his last calamity? ah, heart overgreatly cruel.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:60" n="4">that you have contempt for a suppliant’s voice in his last calamity? ah, heart overgreatly cruel.</l>

lines.text: You who dwell on Helicon Hill, sprung from Urania, who carry off the gentle virgin to her mate, O Hymenaeus Hymen, O Hymen Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="1">You who dwell on Helicon Hill, sprung from Urania, who carry off the gentle virgin to her mate, O Hymenaeus Hymen, O Hymen Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Twine round your temples sweet-smelling flowers of marjoram; put on your gold-tinted veil; lighthearted here, come here, bearing on snowy foot the golden-yellow sandal:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="6">Twine round your temples sweet-smelling flowers of marjoram; put on your gold-tinted veil; lighthearted here, come here, bearing on snowy foot the golden-yellow sandal:</l>

lines.text: And afire with the joyous day, chanting wedding melodies with ringing voice, strike the ground with your feet, with your hand swing aloft the torch of pine.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="11">And afire with the joyous day, chanting wedding melodies with ringing voice, strike the ground with your feet, with your hand swing aloft the torch of pine.</l>

lines.text: For Vinia—fair as Venus dwelling in Idalium when came to the Phrygian judge—a virgin fair, weds Manlius amid happy auspices.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="16">For Vinia—fair as <persName><surname>Venus</surname></persName> dwelling in <placeName key="tgn,7002336">Idalium</placeName> when came to the Phrygian judge—a virgin fair, weds Manlius amid happy auspices.</l>

lines.text: She, bright-shining as the Asian myrtle florid in its branches, which the Hamadryads nurture for their pleasure with besprinkled dew.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="21">She, bright-shining as the Asian myrtle florid in its branches, which the Hamadryads nurture for their pleasure with besprinkled dew.</l>

lines.text: So come then! convey your approach here, leaving the Aonian cave in cliffs of Thespiae, over which flows the chilling stream of Aganippe.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="26">So come then! convey your approach here, leaving the Aonian cave in cliffs of <placeName key="tgn,5004258">Thespiae</placeName>, over which flows the chilling stream of Aganippe.</l>

lines.text: And summon homewards the mistress, eager for her new husband, firm-prisoning her soul in love; as tight-clasping ivy, wandering here and there, wraps the tree around.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="31">And summon homewards the mistress, eager for her new husband, firm-prisoning her soul in love; as tight-clasping ivy, wandering here and there, wraps the tree around.</l>

lines.text: And also you, upright virgins, for whom a like day is nearing, chant in cadence, singing O Hymenaeus Hymen, O Hymen Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="36">And also you, upright virgins, for whom a like day is nearing, chant in cadence, singing <q rend="double">O Hymenaeus Hymen, O Hymen Hymenaeus!</q></l>

lines.text: That more freely, hearing himself to his duty called, will he bear here his presence, Lord of honorable love, uniter of true lovers.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="41">That more freely, hearing himself to his duty called, will he bear here his presence, Lord of honorable love, uniter of true lovers.</l>

lines.text: What god is worthier to be sought by anxious lovers? Whom of the celestials do men worship more greatly? O Hymenaeus Hymen, O Hymen Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="46">What god is worthier to be sought by anxious lovers? Whom of the celestials do men worship more greatly? O Hymenaeus Hymen, O Hymen Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: You for his young the trembling father beseeches, for you virgins unclasp the belt from their breasts, for you the fearful bridegroom harkens with eager ear.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="51">You for his young the trembling father beseeches, for you virgins unclasp the belt from their breasts, for you the fearful bridegroom harkens with eager ear.</l>

lines.text: You deliver into the hands of the untamed youth that flower-like maiden, taken from her mother’s bosom, O Hymenaeus Hymen, O Hymen Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="56">You deliver into the hands of the untamed youth that flower-like maiden, taken from her mother’s bosom, O Hymenaeus Hymen, O Hymen Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Without you Venus can do nothing suitable that good repute sanctions; but she can, with you willing. Who dares to be compared with such a god?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="61">Without you Venus can do nothing suitable that good repute sanctions; but she can, with you willing. Who dares to be compared with such a god?</l>

lines.text: Without you, no house can produce heirs, no parent be surrounded by offspring; but they can, with you willing. Who dares to be compared with such a god?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="66">Without you, no house can produce heirs, no parent be surrounded by offspring; but they can, with you willing. Who dares to be compared with such a god?</l>

lines.text: And lacking your rites no land can give protection to its territory; but it can, with you willing. Who dares to be compared with such a god?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="71">And lacking your rites no land can give protection to its territory; but it can, with you willing. Who dares to be compared with such a god?</l>

lines.text: Unbolt, open the gates: the virgin is here. See how the torches shake their gleaming locks?
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="76">Unbolt, open the gates: the virgin is here. See how the torches shake their gleaming locks?</l>
<l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="79"><gap reason="lost" rend=" * * * "/><lb/><gap reason="lost" rend=" * * * "/></l>

lines.text: Her natural modesty detains her: hearing this the more, she weeps because she must go.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="83">Her natural modesty detains her: hearing this the more, she weeps because she must go.</l>

lines.text: Cease your tears. For you there is no peril, Aurunculeia, that any woman more beauteous will ever see the light of day coming from Ocean.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="86">Cease your tears. For you there is no peril, Aurunculeia, that any woman more beauteous will ever see the light of day coming from Ocean.</l>

lines.text: You are like the hyacinth flower, which stands aloft amid varied riches of its master’s garden. But you delay, day slips by: advance, new bride.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="91">You are like the hyacinth flower, which stands aloft amid varied riches of its master’s garden. But you delay, day slips by: advance, new bride.</l>

lines.text: Advance, new bride, it now seems right, and listen to our speech. See how the torches shake their glittering tresses: advance, new bride.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="96">Advance, new bride, it now seems right, and listen to our speech. See how the torches shake their glittering tresses: advance, new bride.</l>

lines.text: Nor is your man a fickle husband, given to ill adulteries, seeking shameless acts, ever wishing to lie away from your soft breasts,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="101">Nor is your man a fickle husband, given to ill adulteries, seeking shameless acts, ever wishing to lie away from your soft breasts,</l>

lines.text: But as the lithe vine among neighbouring trees doth cling, so shall he be enclasped in your embrace. But day slips by: advance, new bride.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="106">But as the lithe vine among neighbouring trees doth cling, so shall he be enclasped in your embrace. But day slips by: advance, new bride.</l>

lines.text: O nuptial couch which for all * * * * with feet of ivory white.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="111">O nuptial couch which for all <gap reason="lost" rend=" * * * * "/> with feet of ivory white.</l>

lines.text: What joys are coming to your man in fleeting night, in noon of day, let him rejoice! but day slips by: advance, new bride.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="116">What joys are coming to your man in fleeting night, in noon of day, let him rejoice! but day slips by: advance, new bride.</l>

lines.text: Raise high, O boys, the torches: I see the gleaming veil approach. Come, chant in cadence, O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="121">Raise high, O boys, the torches: I see the gleaming veil approach. Come, chant in cadence, <q rend="double">O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus.</q></l>

lines.text: Nor longer silent is lewd Fescinnine jest, nor, favorite, hearing your master’s love has flown, deny the nuts to the boys.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="126">Nor longer silent is lewd Fescinnine jest, nor, favorite, hearing your master’s love has flown, deny the nuts to the boys.</l>

lines.text: Give nuts to the boys, O listless favorite; long enough have you played nuts: now you must serve Talassius. O favorite, give the nuts!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="131">Give nuts to the boys, O listless favorite; long enough have you played nuts: now you must serve Talassius. O favorite, give the nuts!</l>

lines.text: The country wives were dirt to you, O favorite, but yesterday: now the barber shaves your face. Wretched, wretched favorite, give the nuts.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="136">The country wives were dirt to you, O favorite, but yesterday: now the barber shaves your face. Wretched, wretched favorite, give the nuts.</l>

lines.text: They will say when the bridegroom has been annointed that you can scarce abstain from your hairless boys: but abstain! O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="141">They will say when the bridegroom has been annointed that you can scarce abstain from your hairless boys: but abstain! O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus.</l>

lines.text: We know that these delights were known to you only when lawful: but to the wedded these same no more are lawful. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="146">We know that these delights were known to you only when lawful: but to the wedded these same no more are lawful. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: You also, bride, what your husband seeks beware of denying, lest he go elsewhere in its search. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="151">You also, bride, what your husband seeks beware of denying, lest he go elsewhere in its search. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Look, your husband’s home is yours, influential and goodly, allow it to serve you (O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!)
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="156">Look, your husband’s home is yours, influential and goodly, allow it to serve you (O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!)</l>

lines.text: Until white-haired old age, shaking your trembling brow, nods assent to everything. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="161">Until white-haired old age, shaking your trembling brow, nods assent to everything. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Bring with good omen your golden feet across the threshold, and go through the polished doorway. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="166">Bring with good omen your golden feet across the threshold, and go through the polished doorway. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Look! your husband alone within, lying on Tyrian couch, all-expectant waits for you. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="171">Look! your husband alone within, lying on Tyrian couch, all-expectant waits for you. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: No less than in yours, in his breast burns an inmost flame, but more deeply inward. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="176">No less than in yours, in his breast burns an inmost flame, but more deeply inward. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Release the maiden’s slender arm, boy with crimson-bordered toga: now let her approach her husband’s couch. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="181">Release the maiden’s slender arm, boy with crimson-bordered toga: now let her approach her husband’s couch. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus.</l>

lines.text: You good women of fair renown to aged spouses, put the maiden to bed. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="186">You good women of fair renown to aged spouses, put the maiden to bed. O Hymen Hymenaeus io, O Hymen Hymenaeus.</l>

lines.text: Now you may come, bridegroom: your wife is in the bedroom, with face brightly blushing as white parthenice amid ruddy poppies.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="191">Now you may come, bridegroom: your wife is in the bedroom, with face brightly blushing as white parthenice amid ruddy poppies.</l>

lines.text: But, bridegroom (so help me the heaven-dwellers) in no way less beautiful are you, nor does Venus slight you. But the day slips by: on! do not delay.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="196">But, bridegroom (so help me the heaven-dwellers) in no way less beautiful are you, nor does Venus slight you. But the day slips by: on! do not delay.</l>

lines.text: You have not delayed for long, now you are coming. Kindly Venus will help you, since what you desire you take publicly, and do not conceal true love.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="201">You have not delayed for long, now you are coming. Kindly Venus will help you, since what you desire you take publicly, and do not conceal true love.</l>

lines.text: Whoever wishes to keep count of your many thousand games, first let him make an accounting of the number of Africa’s sands and the glittering stars.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="206">Whoever wishes to keep count of your many thousand games, first let him make an accounting of the number of <placeName key="tgn,2086787">Africa</placeName>’s sands and the glittering stars.</l>

lines.text: Play as you like, and speedily give heirs. It does not become so old a name to without children, but from similar stock always to be generated.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="211">Play as you like, and speedily give heirs. It does not become so old a name to without children, but from similar stock always to be generated.</l>

lines.text: A little Torquatus I wish, from his mother’s lap reaching out his dainty hands, and smiling sweetly at his father with lips apart.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="216">A little Torquatus I wish, from his mother’s lap reaching out his dainty hands, and smiling sweetly at his father with lips apart.</l>

lines.text: May he be like his father Manlius, and easily acknowledged by every stranger, and by his face point out his mother’s faithfulness.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="221">May he be like his father <persName><surname>Manlius</surname></persName>, and easily acknowledged by every stranger, and by his face point out his mother’s faithfulness.</l>

lines.text: May such praise confirm his birth from true mother, such fame as rests only with Telemachus from best of mothers, Penelope.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="226">May such praise confirm his birth from true mother, such fame as rests only with Telemachus from best of mothers, Penelope.</l>

lines.text: Close the doors, virgins: enough we’ve played. But, fair bride and groom, live you well, and diligently fulfil the office of vigorous youth.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:61" n="231">Close the doors, virgins: enough we’ve played. But, fair bride and groom, live you well, and diligently fulfil the office of vigorous youth.</l>

lines.text: Vesper is here: youths, arise. Vesper at last has just borne aloft in the heavens his long awaited light. Now it is time to arise, now to leave the luxurious tables, now will come the virgin, now will be sung the Hymenaeus. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="1"><persName><surname>Vesper</surname></persName> is here: youths, arise. <persName><surname>Vesper</surname></persName> at last has just borne aloft in the heavens his long awaited light. Now it is time to arise, now to leave the luxurious tables, now will come the virgin, now will be sung the Hymenaeus. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Unwedded girls, do you see the youths? Arise in response: so it must be that the Star of Eve displays its Oetaean fires. Surely it is thus; see how fleetly they have leapt forth? Nor without intent have they leapt forth; what they will sing, it is our task to surpass. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="6">Unwedded girls, do you see the youths? Arise in response: so it must be that the Star of Eve displays its Oetaean fires. Surely it is thus; see how fleetly they have leapt forth? Nor without intent have they leapt forth; what they will sing, it is our task to surpass. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: For us, comrades, the palm of victory is not easily acquired; see how the girls rehearse what they planned. They do not plan in vain, what they have may be memorable. No wonder: for inwardly they toil with whole of their minds.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="11">For us, comrades, the palm of victory is not easily acquired; see how the girls rehearse what they planned. They do not plan in vain, what they have may be memorable. No wonder: for inwardly they toil with whole of their minds.</l>

lines.text: Our minds are parted in one direction, our ears in another: rightfully therefore we shall be surpassed, for victory loves solicitude. So then, at least now focus your attention: now they begin to sing, now we shall have to respond. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="15">Our minds are parted in one direction, our ears in another: rightfully therefore we shall be surpassed, for victory loves solicitude. So then, at least now focus your attention: now they begin to sing, now we shall have to respond. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Hesperus! what crueler star is borne aloft in the heavens? you who could pluck a maid from her mother’s embrace, pluck a clinging maid from her mother’s embrace, and could give the chaste girl to a burning youth. What more cruel could victors accomplish in vanquished city? Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="20"><persName><surname>Hesperus</surname></persName>! what crueler star is borne aloft in the heavens? you who could pluck a maid from her mother’s embrace, pluck a clinging maid from her mother’s embrace, and could give the chaste girl to a burning youth. What more cruel could victors accomplish in vanquished city? Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Hesperus! what more delightful star shines in the heavens? you who strengthen with your flame the marriage betrothals which husbands pledge, and which the fathers pledged before, and they are not joined before your flame is borne aloft. What more wished for do the gods give than that happy hour? Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="26"><persName><surname>Hesperus</surname></persName>! what more delightful star shines in the heavens? you who strengthen with your flame the marriage betrothals which husbands pledge, and which the fathers pledged before, and they are not joined before your flame is borne aloft. What more wished for do the gods give than that happy hour? Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Hesperus, comrades, has stolen one girl away from us, [...] [Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!]
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="32"><persName><surname>Hesperus</surname></persName>, comrades, has stolen one girl away from us,<gap reason="omitted"/>[Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!]</l>

lines.text: For at your approach a guard always keeps watch. Thieves lie in wait by night, often on your return with your name changed,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="33">For at your approach a guard always keeps watch. Thieves lie in wait by night, often on your return with your name changed,</l>

lines.text: Hesperus, you catch the same men. Yet it pleases the unwedded girls to criticize you with false complaints. But what if they criticize the one whom with silent mind they long for? Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="35"><persName><surname>Hesperus</surname></persName>, you catch the same men. Yet it pleases the unwedded girls to criticize you with false complaints. But what if they criticize the one whom with silent mind they long for? Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: As grows the hidden flower in a walled garden, unknown to cattle, uprooted by no plow, which the breezes caress, the sun strengthens, and the rain gives growth: many boys and many girls have longed for it: this same flower when plucked by a delicate fingernail sheds its blossoms: no boys and no girls long for it:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="39">As grows the hidden flower in a walled garden, unknown to cattle, uprooted by no plow, which the breezes caress, the sun strengthens, and the rain gives growth: many boys and many girls have longed for it: this same flower when plucked by a delicate fingernail sheds its blossoms: no boys and no girls long for it:</l>

lines.text: so the virgin, while she stays untouched, so long is she dear to her own; when she has lost her chaste flower from her body profaned, she does not remain a delight for the boys, she beauteous, nor is she dear to the girls. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="45">so the virgin, while she stays untouched, so long is she dear to her own; when she has lost her chaste flower from her body profaned, she does not remain a delight for the boys, she beauteous, nor is she dear to the girls. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: As the widowed vine which grows in naked field never uplifts itself, never ripens a mellow grape, but bending prone beneath the weight of its tender body now and again its highmost shoot touches with its root; this no farmer, no oxen will cultivate: but if this same chance to be joined with marital elm,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="49">As the widowed vine which grows in naked field never uplifts itself, never ripens a mellow grape, but bending prone beneath the weight of its tender body now and again its highmost shoot touches with its root; this no farmer, no oxen will cultivate: but if this same chance to be joined with marital elm,</l>

lines.text: many farmers, many oxen will cultivate it: so the virgin, while she stays untouched, so long does she age, uncultivated; but when she obtains fitting union at the right time, dearer is she to her husband and less of a trouble to her father. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="55">many farmers, many oxen will cultivate it: so the virgin, while she stays untouched, so long does she age, uncultivated; but when she obtains fitting union at the right time, dearer is she to her husband and less of a trouble to her father. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Even you, virgin, do not struggle against such a mate. It is improper to struggle with him to whom your father has handed you over, your father himself together with your mother whom you must obey. Your maidenhead is not wholly yours, in part it is your parents’: a third part is your father’s, a third part is given to your mother, a third alone is yours: be unwilling to struggle against two,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="59">Even you, virgin, do not struggle against such a mate. It is improper to struggle with him to whom your father has handed you over, your father himself together with your mother whom you must obey. Your maidenhead is not wholly yours, in part it is your parents’: a third part is your father’s, a third part is given to your mother, a third alone is yours: be unwilling to struggle against two,</l>

lines.text: who to their son-in-law their rights together with dowry have given. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:62" n="65">who to their son-in-law their rights together with dowry have given. Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!</l>

lines.text: Over the vast main borne by swift-sailing ship, Attis, as with hasty hurried foot he reached the Phrygian wood and gained the tree-girt gloomy sanctuary of the Goddess,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:63" n="1">Over the vast main borne by swift-sailing ship, Attis, as with hasty hurried foot he reached the Phrygian wood and gained the tree-girt gloomy sanctuary of the Goddess,</l>

lines.text: there roused by rabid rage and mind astray, with sharp-edged flint downwards dashed his burden of virility.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:63" n="4">there roused by rabid rage and mind astray, with sharp-edged flint downwards dashed his burden of virility.</l>

lines.text: Then as he felt his limbs were left without their manhood, and the fresh-spilt blood staining the soil, with bloodless hand she hastily took a tambour light to hold, your taborine, Cybele, your initiate rite,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:63" n="6">Then as he felt his limbs were left without their manhood, and the fresh-spilt blood staining the soil, with bloodless hand she hastily took a tambour light to hold, your taborine, Cybele, your initiate rite,</l>

lines.text: and with feeble fingers beating the hollowed bullock’s back, she rose up quivering thus to chant to her companions. Haste you together, she-priests, to Cybele’s dense woods, together haste, you vagrant herd of the dame Dindymene, you who inclining towards strange places as exiles,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:63" n="10">and with feeble fingers beating the hollowed bullock’s back, she rose up quivering thus to chant to her companions. <q rend="double">Haste you together, she-priests, to Cybele’s dense woods, together haste, you vagrant herd of the dame Dindymene, you who inclining towards strange places as exiles,</q></l>

lines.text: following in my footsteps, led by me, comrades, you who have faced the ravening sea and truculent main, and have castrated your bodies in your utmost hate of Venus, make glad our mistress speedily with your minds’ mad wanderings. Let dull delay depart from your thoughts, together haste you, follow
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:63" n="15"><q rend="double; merge">following in my footsteps, led by me, comrades, you who have faced the ravening sea and truculent main, and have castrated your bodies in your utmost hate of <persName><surname>Venus</surname></persName>, make glad our mistress speedily with your minds’ mad wanderings. Let dull delay depart from your thoughts, together haste you, follow</q> </l>

lines.text: to the Phrygian home of Cybele, to the Phrygian woods of the Goddess, where sounds the cymbal’s voice, where the tambour resounds, where the Phrygian flutist pipes deep notes on the curved reed, where the ivy-clad Maenades furiously toss their heads, where they enact their sacred orgies with shrill-sounding ululations,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:63" n="20"><q rend="double; merge">to the Phrygian home of Cybele, to the Phrygian woods of the Goddess, where sounds the cymbal’s voice, where the tambour resounds, where the Phrygian flutist pipes deep notes on the curved reed, where the ivy-clad Maenades furiously toss their heads, where they enact their sacred orgies with shrill-sounding ululations,</q></l>

lines.text: where that wandering band of the Goddess flits about: there it is meet to hasten with hurried mystic dance. When Attis, spurious woman, had thus chanted to her comity, the chorus straightway shrills with trembling tongues, the light tambour booms, the concave cymbals clang,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:63" n="25"><q rend="double; merge">where that wandering band of the Goddess flits about: there it is meet to hasten with hurried mystic dance.</q> When Attis, spurious woman, had thus chanted to her comity, the chorus straightway shrills with trembling tongues, the light tambour booms, the concave cymbals clang,</l>

lines.text: and the troop swiftly hastes with rapid feet to verdurous Ida. Then raging wildly, breathless, wandering, with brain distraught, hurries Attis with her tambour, their leader through dense woods, like an untamed heifer shunning the burden of the yoke: and the swift Gallae press behind their speedy-footed leader.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:63" n="30">and the troop swiftly hastes with rapid feet to verdurous Ida. Then raging wildly, breathless, wandering, with brain distraught, hurries Attis with her tambour, their leader through dense woods, like an untamed heifer shunning the burden of the yoke: and the swift Gallae press behind their speedy-footed leader.</l>

lines.text: So when the home of Cybele they reach, wearied out with excess of toil and lack of food they fall in slumber. Sluggish sleep shrouds their eyes drooping with faintness, and raging fury leaves their minds to quiet ease. But when the sun with radiant eyes from face of gold
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:63" n="35">So when the home of Cybele they reach, wearied out with excess of toil and lack of food they fall in slumber. Sluggish sleep shrouds their eyes drooping with faintness, and raging fury leaves their minds to quiet ease. But when the sun with radiant eyes from face of gold</l>

lines.text: glanced over the white heavens, the firm soil, and the savage sea, and drove away the glooms of night with his brisk and clamorous team, then sleep fast-flying quickly sped away from wakening Attis, and goddess Pasithea received Somnus in her panting bosom. Then when from quiet rest torn, her delirium over,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:63" n="40">glanced over the white heavens, the firm soil, and the savage sea, and drove away the glooms of night with his brisk and clamorous team, then sleep fast-flying quickly sped away from wakening Attis, and goddess Pasithea received Somnus in her panting bosom. Then when from quiet rest torn, her delirium over,</l>

lines.text: Attis at once recalled to mind her deed, and with lucid thought saw what she had lost, and where she stood, with heaving heart she backwards traced her steps to the landing-place. There, gazing over the vast main with tear-filled eyes, with saddened voice in tristful soliloquy thus did she lament her land:
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:63" n="45">Attis at once recalled to mind her deed, and with lucid thought saw what she had lost, and where she stood, with heaving heart she backwards traced her steps to the landing-place. There, gazing over the vast main with tear-filled eyes, with saddened voice in tristful soliloquy thus did she lament her land:</l>

lines.text: Mother-land, my creatress, mother-land, my begetter, which full sadly I’m forsaking, as runaway serfs do from their lords, to the woods of Ida I have hasted on foot, to stay amid snow and icy dens of beasts, and to wander through their hidden lurking-places full of fury.

lines.text: Where, or in what part, mother-land, may I imagine that you are? My very eyeball craves to fix its glance towards you, while for a brief space my mind is freed from wild ravings. And must I wander over these woods far from my home? From country, goods, friends, and parents, must I be parted?

lines.text: Leave the forum, the palaestra, the race-course, and gymnasium? Wretched, wretched soul, it is yours to grieve for ever and ever. For what shape is there, whose kind I have not worn? lines.text: for while their eager desire strives for its end, nothing fear they to swear, nothing of promises forbear they: but instantly their lusting thoughts are satiate with lewdness, nothing of speech they remember, nothing of perjuries care. lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:64" n="145"><q rend="double; merge">for while their eager desire strives for its end, nothing fear they to swear, nothing of promises forbear they: but instantly their lusting thoughts are satiate with lewdness, nothing of speech they remember, nothing of perjuries care. lines.text: preferring to suffer the loss of a brother rather than fail your need in the supreme hour, O ingrate. For which I shall be a gift as prey to be rent by wild beasts and the carrion-fowl, nor dead shall I be placed in the earth, covered with funeral mound. What lioness bore you beneath lonely crag?

lines.text: What sea conceived and spued you from its foamy crest? What Syrtis, what grasping Scylla, what vast Charybdis? O you repayer with such rewards for your sweet life! If it was not your heart’s wish to yoke with me, through holding in horror the dread decrees of my stern sire,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:64" n="155"><q rend="double; merge">What sea conceived and spued you from its foamy crest? What Syrtis, what grasping Scylla, what vast Charybdis? O you repayer with such rewards for your sweet life! If it was not your heart’s wish to yoke with me, through holding in horror the dread decrees of my stern sire,</q></l>

lines.text: yet you could have led me to your home, where as your handmaid I might have served you with cheerful service, laving your snowy feet with clear water, or spreading the purple coverlet over your couch.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:64" n="160"><q rend="double; merge">yet you could have led me to your home, where as your handmaid I might have served you with cheerful service, laving your snowy feet with clear water, or spreading the purple coverlet over your couch.</q></l>

lines.text: Yet why, distraught with woe, do I vainly lament to the unknowing winds, which unfurnished with sense, can neither hear uttered complaints nor can return them? For now he has sped away into the midst of the seas, nor does any mortal appear along this desolate seaboard.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:64" n="164"><q rend="double; merge">Yet why, distraught with woe, do I vainly lament to the unknowing winds, which unfurnished with sense, can neither hear uttered complaints nor can return them? For now he has sped away into the midst of the seas, nor does any mortal appear along this desolate seaboard.</q></l>

lines.text: Thus with overweening scorn bitter Fate in my extreme hour even grudges ears to my complaints. All-powerful Jupiter! would that in old time the Cecropian ships had not touched at the Gnossan shores, nor that the false mariner, bearing the direful ransom to the unquelled bull, had bound his ropes to Crete,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:64" n="169"><q rend="double; merge">Thus with overweening scorn bitter Fate in my extreme hour even grudges ears to my complaints. All-powerful Jupiter! would that in old time the Cecropian ships had not touched at the Gnossan shores, nor that the false mariner, bearing the direful ransom to the unquelled bull, had bound his ropes to <placeName key="tgn,7012056">Crete</placeName>,</q></l>

lines.text: nor that yonder wretch hiding ruthless designs beneath sweet seemings had reposed as a guest in our halls! For whither may I flee? in what hope, O lost one, take refuge? Shall I climb the Idomenean crags? but the truculent sea stretching far off with its whirlings of waters separates us.
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:64" n="175"><q rend="double; merge">nor that yonder wretch hiding ruthless designs beneath sweet seemings had reposed as a guest in our halls! For whither may I flee? in what hope, O lost one, take refuge? Shall I climb the Idomenean crags? but the truculent sea stretching far off with its whirlings of waters separates us.</q></l>

lines.text: Dare I hope for help from my father, whom I deserted to follow a youth besprinkled with my brother’s blood? Can I crave comfort from the care of a faithful husband, who is fleeing with yielding oars, encurving amidst whirling waters? If I turn from the beach there is no roof in this tenantless island,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:64" n="180"><q rend="double; merge">Dare I hope for help from my father, whom I deserted to follow a youth besprinkled with my brother’s blood? If I turn from the beach there is no roof in this tenantless island,</q></l>

lines.text: no way shows a passage, circled by waves of the sea; no way of flight, no hope; all denotes dumbness, desolation, and death. Nevertheless my eyes shall not be dimmed in death, nor my senses secede from my spent frame,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:64" n="185"><q rend="double; merge">no way shows a passage, circled by waves of the sea; no way of flight, no hope; all denotes dumbness, desolation, and death. lines.text: until I have besought from the gods a just penalty for my betrayal, and implored the faith of the celestials with my last breath. Wherefore you requiters of men’s deeds with avenging pains, O Eumenides, whose front enwreathed with serpent-locks blazons the wrath exhaled from your bosom,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:64" n="190"><q rend="double; merge">until I have besought from the gods a just penalty for my betrayal, and implored the faith of the celestials with my last breath. lines.text: come here, here, listen to my complaint, which I, sad wretch, am urged to outpour from my innermost marrow, helpless, burning, and blind with frenzied fury. And since in truth they spring from the very depths of my heart, be unwilling to allow my agony to pass unheeded,
lines.xml: <l xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" xml:base="urn:cts:latinLit:phi0472.phi001.perseus-eng4:64" n="195"><q rend="double; merge">come here, here, listen to my complaint, which I, sad wretch, am urged to outpour from my innermost marrow, helpless, burning, and blind with frenzied fury.
